Differences in macrophage pyroptosis 
and polarization induced by nano-/
micro-calcium oxalate crystals
Xin-Yi Tong1, Wei-Jian Nong1, Run-Min Tan1 and Jian-Ming Ouyang1* 

Abstract 
Objective  This study aimed to compare the differences in pyroptosis and polarization of macrophages induced 
by different sizes of calcium oxalate monohydrate (COM) crystals and discuss the mechanism of kidney stone 
formation.

Methods  COM crystals with sizes of about 100 nm, 500 nm, 2.5 μm, and 10 μm were synthesized and characterized. 
THP-1 cells were induced to differentiate into macrophage-like cells. The damage of COM crystals to Mφs was evalu-
ated by CCK-8 assay. The activation of the pyroptosis signaling pathway, cell morphology, and proportion of pyrop-
tosis cells in Mφs induced by COM crystals were detected. Finally, the proportion of M1/M2 polarization was qualita-
tively and quantitatively assessed.

Results  COM-100 nm, COM-500 nm, COM-2.5 μm, and COM-10 μm all significantly induced the pyroptosis and polar-
ization of Mφs. Among them, at the same cell viability, COM-10 μm induced the highest pyroptosis rate. The expres-
sion of NLRP3 and GSDMD-N induced by COM-10 μm increased by 81.43 ± 11.45% and 112.00 ± 9.87%, respectively, 
and the rate of caspase-1/PI double-positive pyroptosis cells was 22.2%. Meanwhile, COM-10 μm induced the highest 
proportion of M1 polarization (M1/M2 ratio was 209.90% ± 2.54%).

Conclusion  COM-10 μm significantly activates the classical caspase-1-mediated pyroptosis pathway and promotes 
M1 polarization in Mφs. Therefore, at the same cell viability, large-sized micro-COM is more capable of inducing 
inflammation than nano-COM.

Keywords  Pyroptosis, Macrophages, Polarization, Inflammation, Calcium oxalate crystals

Introduction
The  kidneys  are  responsible  for  filtering  waste  from  the 
blood. Although tiny particles pass through the collecting 
tubules of the kidneys on a daily basis, most particles are 
successfully excreted through urine. When calcium oxa-
late  monohydrate  (COM)  crystals  grow,  aggregate,  and 
precipitate  in  the  urinary  system,  and  form  obstruction 
in the collecting tubules [1], calcium oxalate stone forma-
tion may be induced.

Macrophages  (Mφs)  are  immune  cells  with  strong 
phagocytic  function  in  the  human  body.  In  the  kidney, 
Mφs have demonstrated the ability to detect and phago-
cytose  small  particles  [1].  He  et  al.  [1]  found  that  Mφs 
protrude  from  the  inner  wall  of  mouse  renal  tubules, 
awaiting and digesting passing particles. Okada et al. [2] 
demonstrated that COM crystals of 1 μm in length were 
degraded  by  lysosomes  upon  phagocytosis  by  Mφs,  and 
this process lasted about 6 days. The key role of Mφs in 
COM crystallization has led to the realization that it may 

be  possible  to  prevent  the  formation  and  recurrence  of 
kidney  stones  in  individuals  by  regulating  the  immune 
response  [3].  Studies  have  shown  that  COM  crystals 
activate  Mφs  to  polarize  into  M1  Mφs  (also  known 
as  pro-inflammatory  Mφs),  promote  the  production  of 
inflammatory factors [4], and facilitate Mφs recruitment 
[5].

As  a  form  of  programmed  cell  death,  pyroptosis  has 
unique  morphological  and  mechanistic  characteristics 
and  is  closely  related  to  the  inflammatory  response  [6]. 
Among  them,  the  classical  pyroptosis  pathway  has  been 
extensively  studied.  In  the  classical  pyroptosis  pathway, 
NOD-like  receptor  thermal  protein  domain-associated 
protein  3  (NLRP3),  apoptosis-associated  speck-like  pro-
tein containing CARD (ASC), and pro-caspase-1 assem-
ble  to  form  an  inflammasome,  activating  pro-caspase-1, 
which  is  cleaved  into  p20  and  p10  fragments  [7].  Acti-
vated  caspase-1  cleaves  pro-interleukin-1  beta  (pro-
IL-1β)  and  gasdermin-D  (GSDMD)  into  their  active

forms,  IL-1β  and  the  N-terminal  cleavage  product  of 
gasdermin-D  (GSDMD-N);  GSDMD-N  oligomerizes  to 
produce membrane pores that allow the release of IL-1β 
from the cell [6, 7].

A number of studies have demonstrated the important 
role  of  pyroptosis  in  crystalline  nephropathy.  Inflamma-
tion  mediated  by  cell–crystal  interactions  can  lead  to 
inflammatory damage of renal cells; promote the expres-
sion  of  intracellular  NADPH  oxidase;  induce  the  exten-
sive production of reactive oxygen species (ROS); activate 
the  NLRP3  inflammasome;  excrete  a  large  number  of 
inflammatory  factors;  trigger  an  inflammatory  cascade; 
promote  the  aggregation,  nucleation,  and  growth  of 
COM; and eventually lead to the development of intrare-
nal crystals and even stones [8].

Small-sized  crystals  (such  as  nanoscale  particles)  are 
easily  ingested  by  immune  cells  (such  as  macrophages) 
through  endocytosis  [9];  particles  smaller  than  1  μm 
are  efficiently  phagocytized  and  cleared,  thereby  reduc-
ing  inflammatory  responses  [10].  Large  crystals,  such 
as  micron-sized  particles,  are  primarily  internalized  by 
immune  cells  via  phagocytosis  and  frustrated  phagocy-
tosis [11], which may lead to proinflammatory responses 
or excessive immune activation and trigger strong proin-
flammatory  responses  by  activating  signaling  pathways 
such  as  the  NLRP3  inflammasome.  In  crystal-related 
diseases  (such  as  gout  and  kidney  stones),  large  crys-
tal particles may be closely related to tissue damage and 
inflammation [12].

Chen  et  al.  [13]  showed  that  monosodium  urate  crys-
tals  are  one  of  the  pathogenic  factors  of  gout,  and  long 
monosodium  urate  crystals  are  more  toxic  than  short 
monosodium  urate  crystals  in  inducing  pyroptosis  in 
neutrophils  and  macrophages  [13].  Small  monosodium 
urate  crystals  are  readily  phagocytosed  by  macrophages 
but usually do not cause a strong inflammatory response. 
By  contrast,  large  monosodium  urate  crystals  stimulate 
macrophages to release proinflammatory cytokines such 
as IL-1β, which triggers a severe inflammatory response 
and  leads  to  an  acute  gout  attack.  Maintaining  mono-
sodium  urate  crystals  below  0.5  μm  can  prevent  gout 
attacks [10]. Zieren et al. [14] showed that asbestos fibers 
need to be at least  4  μm in length to  cause  a  significant 
inflammatory response [10]. In the study of fibers, Sand-
ers et al. [15] showed that large fibers may induce a large 
fibrous  capsule,  whereas  the  inflammatory  response  of 
fibers below 6 μm appeared diminished.

Nevertheless, the degree of inflammation varies in cor-
relation  with  the  dimensions  of  the  material  across  dif-
ferent disease models, and it is influenced by the material 
and  the  cell  line  being  studied.  Breisch  et  al.  [16]  dem-
onstrated  via  in  vitro  cell  culture  analysis  that  the  size, 
shape,  and  crystal  structure  of  granular   TiO2  particles 

with  the  same  chemical  properties  do  not  influence  the 
biological  effects  studied.  The  study  by  Petushkov  et  al. 
[17]  indicted  that  the  cytotoxicity  of  nanoscale  silicalite 
is complex and depends on the particle size, surface func-
tional  group,  and  cell  line  used  for  the  toxicity  studies; 
the variations in toxicity among cell types are most likely 
due to the different mechanisms for nanoparticle uptake 
by  the  HEK293  and  RAW264.7  cell  lines.  The  study  of 
Ewence  et  al.  [18]  showed  that  in  macrophages,  crys-
tals of 1–2 μm in diameter were more potent than large 
crystals  15  μm)  in  inducing  the  release  of  proinflamma-
tory  cytokines.  Sun  et  al.  [19]  showed  that  the  toxicity 
of  hydroxyapatite  crystals  to  HK-2  cells  increases  as  the 
crystal size decreases.

The crystal size-dependent immune response may play 
an  important  role  in  the  occurrence  and  development 
of  kidney  stones.  However,  the  effect  of  calcium  oxalate 
monohydrate (COM) crystal size on Mφs damage in the 
field  of  kidney  stone  research  remains  unclear,  particu-
larly  regarding  the  phagocytic  ability  of  Mφs  on  COM 
crystals  of  different  sizes  and  the  relationship  between 
COM crystal size and Mφs pyroptosis. In this study, the 
effects  of  COM  crystals  with  sizes  of  100  nm,  500  nm, 
3  μm,  and  10  μm  on  the  pyroptosis  and  polarization  of 
macrophages  were  investigated.  This  work  will  help 
understand the differences in macrophage injury, inflam-
mation,  and  immune  response  caused  by  different  sizes 
of urinary microcrystals, thereby offering insights for the 
future  application  of  inhibitors  to  regulate  crystal  size 
and design effective anti-calculus drugs.

Urine  contains  microcrystals  of  different  sizes  and 
morphologies  because  of  the  difference  in  super-
saturation  of  lithogenic  salts,  viscosity,  and  pH  levels 
among  individuals.  Crystal  size  and  crystal  morphol-
ogy  can  affect  cytotoxicity.  Our  previous  studies  on 
COM crystals have shown that the difference in cyto-
toxicity  caused  by  size  is  greater  than  that  caused 
bymorphology [20, 21].

The  formation  of  kidney  stones  includes  processes 
such  as  nucleation,  growth,  aggregation,  and  adhesion 
of stone crystals [22]. The first step of urinary stone for-
mation is the nucleation of urinary mineral (e.g., CaOx) 
from  supersaturated  urine.  The  formed  nuclei  (gener-
ally less than 10 nm) grow and/or aggregate to a patho-
logical size (several tens of microns). Pathological urinary 
microcrystals retained in the kidney will proliferate and/
or  aggregate,  resulting  in  the  formation  of  stones  (mil-
limeter  scale).  Therefore,  there  is  a  close  relationship 
between the size of urinary crystals and the formation of 
kidney stones. In our previous clinical investigation [23], 
we  found  that  90%  of  urinary  crystals  in  healthy  people 
were less than 20 μm, and the size was relatively uniform. 
However,  the  size  of  urinary  crystals  in  patients  with

kidney stones varied from 1 μm to 220 μm, and the num-
ber of large urinary crystals was significantly greater than 
that in healthy people.

Our  previous  analysis  of  clinical  samples  revealed  the 
existence of calcium oxalate crystals in the kidney, rang-
ing from the nanometer scale to the micron scale. Thus, 
multiple  gradient  sizes  were  selected  in  this  paper: 
100 nm, 500 nm, 2.5 μm, and 10 μm.

The  effect  of  COM  crystal  morphology  [20]  on  cyto-
toxicity  and  the  difference  between  COM  crystal  and 
calcium  oxalate  dihydrate  (COD)  crystal  are  also  under 
investigation [24].

Some  studies  have  shown  that  differences  in  material 
shape  and  morphology  affect  cytotoxicity,  but  most  are 
due to the difference between rough and smooth surfaces 
of materials [25] and long needle morphology and round 
ball  morphology  [26].  Smooth  titanium  induces  inflam-
matory macrophage (M1-like) activation, as indicated by 
increased levels of interleukins IL-1β, IL-6, and TNFα.

By  contrast,  hydrophilic  rough  titanium  induces  mac-
rophage  activation,  similar  to  the  anti-inflammatory 
M2-like  state,  increasing  interleukin  IL-4  and  IL-10  lev-
els  [25].  Needle-shaped  carbon  nanotubes  and  asbestos 
have been shown to induce IL-1β secretion from human 
monocyte-derived  macrophages  in  ROS  and  cathep-
sin  B/P2X  in  a  NLRP3  activation-dependent  manner. 
In  contrast  to  these  needle-like  materials,  spherical  car-
bon  black  with  an  average  size  of  14  nm  was  ineffective 
for  IL-1β  production  at  the  same  concentration  [25].  In 
other words, we believe that significant differences in the 
roughness,  topography,  and  shape  of  the  materials  will 
lead to significant differences in cytotoxicity.

In  this  study,  the  pyroptosis  and  polarization  of  mac-
rophages  induced  by  COM  crystals  of  100  nm,  500  nm, 
3  μm,  and  10  μm  were  investigated.  Understanding  the 
effect  of  urine  microcrystal  size  on  macrophage  injury 
and  inflammation  is  beneficial.  Effective  inhibitors  that 
can  regulate  the  size  of  urinary  microcrystals  may  be 
developed to reduce the incidence of kidney stones.

Characterization of COM crystals

1)  Crystal morphology and size observed by SEM

  About 1 mg of COM crystals was weighed, dispersed 
in 10 mL of absolute ethanol, and sonicated for 3 min 
to  form  a  suspension.  The  above  suspension  was 
dropped  onto  10  mm × 10  mm  slides  and  dried  at 
50 ℃. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) was used 
to observe the size and morphology of COM crystals. 
Nano Measurer 1.2 software was used to measure the 
size  of  the  photographed  samples,  and  the  statistics 
were normally fitted in Origin (Version 2021, Origin-
Lab Corporation, Northampton, MA, USA) software. 
The size range of the sample was obtained.

2)  X-ray diffraction
  An appropriate amount of COM crystal samples was 
analyzed using an X-ray diffractometer. The test con-
ditions  were  CuKᾱ  rays,  graphite  monochromator, 

30  kV,  25  mA,  scanning  range  of  5–600,  scanning 
speed of 80/min, and step width of 0.020/s.

Cell culture

THP-1  cells  were  cultured  in  RPMI-1640  medium 
containing  10%  fetal  bovine  serum  and  0.05  mM 
β-mercaptoethanol in an incubator at 37 ℃ and 5%  CO2. 
The  medium  was  changed  by  replenishing  or  partially 
exchanging the fluid and passaged by centrifugation.

Macrophage differentiation
Experimental grouping
THP-1  cells  were  plated  at  a  density  of   106  cells/mL. 
The  experiment  was  divided  into  three  groups:  (a)  nor-
mal  control  group  (NC):  THP-1  cells  were  cultured  in 
RPMI-1640  medium  without  serum;  (b)  differentiation 
group:  THP-1  cells  were  induced  to  Mφs  by  incubation 
in  complete  culture  medium  containing  5  ng/mL  PMA 
for 24 h, followed by resting for 24 h [28]; and (c) blank 
background group: serum-free RPMI-1640 medium only.

Microscopic observation of cell morphology 
and hematoxylin–eosin staining (HE staining)

The  experimental  groups  were  the  same  as  the  (a)  nor-
mal  control  group  and  (b)  differentiation  group.  The 
cells were seeded in 12-well plates. After differentiation, 
the  cells  were  photographed  under  an  inverted  fluores-
cence microscope to observe the cell morphology. After 
cell  attachment,  the  original  culture  medium  was  aspi-
rated  and  washed  once  with  PBS.  Each  well  was  fixed 
with 1.5 mL of 4% paraformaldehyde for 15 min, stained 
with  hematoxylin  staining  solution  for  15  min,  rinsed 
with  water  to  remove  excess  staining  solution,  added 
with eosin staining solution to stain for 90 s, rinsed with 
water to remove excess staining solution, observed by an 
inverted  fluorescence  microscope,  and  photographed. 
The nucleus was blue, and the cytoplasm was pink.

Immunofluorescence detection of CD68 expression

The experimental groups were the same as the (a) nor-
mal  control  group  and  (b)  differentiation  group.  After 
cells were seeded on slides and differentiated, the cells 
were  fixed  using  4%  paraformaldehyde  fixative  for 
15 min and then washed three times with PBS. The cells 
were permeabilized for 10 min and washed three times 
with PBS. The cells were blocked with blocking solution 
for 1 h and washed three times with PBS. The cells were 
incubated  at  4  ℃  overnight  after  dilution  of  the  CD68 
primary  antibody  at  the  prescribed  ratio  and  washed 
three  times  with  PBS.  The  cells  were  incubated  for 
70  min  after  dilution  of  the  secondary  antibody  at  the 
prescribed  proportions  and  washed  three  times  with 
PBS. The nuclei were stained with DAPI for 5 min and 
washed  three  times  with  PBS.  Finally,  a  sealing  opera-
tion  was  performed  to  fix  the  slide  containing  cells. 
The  expression  of  CD68  in  the  treated  cell  sheets  was 
observed  by  laser  confocal  microscopy.  The  images  of 
immunofluorescence  were  semiquantitatively  analyzed 
using ImageJ software.

Crystal characterization

1)  XRD characterization

  The  material  composition  and  purity  of  the  sam-
ples were characterized by XRD, as shown in Fig. 2. 
The  XRD  pattern  of  the  sample  was  compared  with 
the  diffraction  data  of  the  COM  crystal  standard 
(JCPDS  card  number  20–231),  and  the  characteris-
tic  peaks  were  consistent.  The  peaks  at  2θ = 14.88°, 
24.2°, 30.16°, 38.24° were assigned to the ( 101 ), (020), 
( 202 ), and (130) crystal planes of COM. The absence 

of other miscellaneous peaks indicated that the syn-
thesized material was a pure COM crystal. The shape 
of the diffraction peak of the sample was sharp, indi-
cating  that  the  product  was  fully  crystallized.  The 
relative intensity of the diffraction peaks fluctuated to 
varying  degrees,  which  was  related  to  the  degree  of 
crystal  crystallization,  the  formation  of  large  micro-
crystals,  or  the  well-ordered  orientation,  further 
proving that the sample size differed.

2)  SEM characterization

  The  structure  and  size  of  the  samples  were  charac-
terized by SEM, as shown in Fig. 2. The synthesized 
COM-100  nm  had  a  smooth  edge,  whereas  COM-
500  nm,  COM-2.5  μm,  and  COM-10  μm  had  elon-
gated hexagons, characteristic of COM crystals [30]. 
The  particle  sizes  of  COM-100  nm,  COM-500  nm, 
COM-2.5 μm, and COM-10 μm were 98.6 ± 1.0 nm, 
439 ± 2 nm, 2.30 ± 0.04 μm, and 10.3 ± 0.2 μm, respec-
tively.
In  summary,  the  size  difference  of  the  synthesized 
COM  crystals  was  obvious,  covering  nanometer 
and  micrometer,  with  a  comparable  magnitude  of 
difference.  The  difference  between  COM-100  nm 
and  COM-500  nm  was  a  factor  of  5,  the  difference 
between COM-500 nm and COM-2.5 μm was a fac-
tor  of  5,  and  the  difference  between  COM-2.5  μm 
and  COM-10  μm  was  a  factor  of  4.  This  size  differ-
ence  is  beneficial  to  explore  the  effect  of  size  factor

Zeta potential of COM crystals

To  explore  the  cause  for  the  high  pyroptosis  rate  of 
COM-100  nm,  we  measured  the  zeta  potential  of  COM 
crystals (Fig. 7).

The  absolute  value  of  the  zeta  potential  on  the  crys-
tal  surface  was  positively  correlated  with  the  stability 
of  the  crystal  suspension.  As  shown  in  Fig.  7A,  the  zeta 
potential values for COM-100 nm, COM-500 nm, COM-
2.5 μm, and COM-10 μm in ethanol were − 0.86 ± 0.11, − 
1.73 ± 0.14, − 12.9 ± 1.5,  and − 15.9 ± 1.0  mV,  respectively. 
As the COM crystal size increased, the absolute value of 
its  zeta  potential  also  rose,  resulting  in  heightened  elec-
trostatic  repulsion  between  crystals,  which  diminished 
their  tendency  to  aggregate  and  enhanced  the  stability 
of  the  crystal  suspension.  As  shown  in  Fig.  7B,  the  zeta 
potential values of the four COM crystals were − 11.00 ± 
0.35, − 8.75 ± 0.54, − 13.30 ± 0.45,  and − 14.267 ± 0.92  mV, 
respectively.  In  general,  the  absolute  value  of  its  zeta 
potential increases with the increase in crystal size. How-
ever, the COM-100 nm crystals demonstrated anomalies, 
possibly due to the enhanced aggregation in RPMI-1640 
medium.

Discussion
Crystal–cell interactions: processes and molecular 
mechanisms

The  interaction  between  COM  crystals  and  cells  is  a 
dynamic process that includes initial adhesion, endocyto-
sis or shedding of the crystals, and downstream response.

1)  COM crystal–cell adhesion: molecular mechanisms.

  The  adherence  of  COM  crystals  to  cells  involves  a 
variety  of  biophysical  mechanisms  and  molecular 
components.

  The  charge  interaction  mediates  the  binding  of 
COM crystal to the cell membrane. This electrostatic 
attraction is the main driving force for adhesion [44]. 
COM crystals with a large  Ca2+ ion-rich ( 101 ) active 
face showed the highest toxicity in HK-2 cells and the 
largest  extent  of  adhesion  onto  the  cell  surface  [45]. 
Non-specific  electrostatic  interactions  between  syn-
thetic  phospholipid  monolayers  and  COM  crystals 
appeared to control the growth of COM crystals with 
defined crystal orientation and morphology [46].

2)  Endocytosis  of  COM  crystals  by  cells:  molecular 

mechanisms.

  Crystalline  water  can  form  hydrogen  bonds  with 
the  phospholipid  head  group  after  combining  with 
COM, and the feasibility of this hydrogen bond net-
work  was  demonstrated  by  structural  visualization 
software. The formation of hydrogen bonds helps sta-
bilize  and  enhance  the  attachment  of  COM  to  lipid 
membranes [55].

  The 

the 

ionic  environment  affects 

interaction 
between  COM  crystals  and  cells  [56].  Calcium  ions 
and  hydrogen  ions  promote  crystal  adhesion  to 
cells.  A  previous  study  reported  that  50  mM  cal-
cium markedly promotes crystal adhesion to cellular 
proteins  [56].  Xiang  et  al.  demonstrated  that   Ca2+ 
treatment  increases  the  expression  levels  of  pyrop-
tosis and adhesion-related proteins [57]. A pH range 
of 4 or 5 is optimal for the binding of COM crystals 
to cellular proteins [56]. A urine pH at the low limit 
observed in humans, i.e., pH 5 (or even slightly less), 
may  predispose  individuals  to  kidney  stone  forma-
tion  by  increasing  the  likelihood  of  calcium  oxalate 
crystal adhesion to cells and subsequent retention in 
the kidneys. Therefore, hypercalciuria and/or an acid 
urine  may  promote  renal  stone  formation  via  unex-
pected  pathways  (i.e.,  crystal  binding  to  cells  rather 
than crystal growth) [56].

  The size of COM crystals can also affect the strength 
of  their  interaction  with  cell  membranes.  Peerapen 
et  al.  [47]  demonstrated  that  COM  crystals  of  vary-
ing sizes exhibit differential adhesive capabilities with 
renal  tubular  epithelial  cells.  Large  crystals  showed 
enhanced  capability  to  bind  onto  the  epithelial  cell 
surface. Their findings were consistent with the clini-
cal  findings  showing  that  the  large  COM  crystals 
were  most  pathogenic  and  were  found  only  in  the 
urine of stone formers [47].

  Cellular injury may promote the interaction of COM 
crystals with cells. Individual cell injury (loss of lipid 
asymmetry)  and  generalized  cell  monolayer  injury 
(loss  of  cell  polarity)  result  in  altered  cell  surface 
presentations,  and  both  forms  of  injury  result  in  an 
increased  affinity  for  crystal  attachment  [58].  The 
crystal-binding  capability  of  injured  Vero  cells  was 
obviously  stronger  than  that  of  the  control  group 
because  of  the  increased  expression  of  negatively 
charged  adhesion  molecules,  such  as  OPN  [59],  in 
the injured Vero cells.

  There  are  significant  differences  in  the  endocytic 
mechanisms of COM crystals with different sizes.
  Nanoscale COM crystals such as 50 and 100 nm may 
rely  on  clathrin-mediated  endocytosis  and  caveolin-
dependent endocytosis [9]. Large micron-sized crys-
tals may be ingested via macropinocytosis or phago-
cytosis [9, 11]. The “frustrated phagocytosis” of large 
particles  (the  inability  of  phagocytes  to  engulf  these 
particles) fosters the formation of giant cells, a poly-
ploid version of proinflammatory macrophages [11].
  The  endocytosed  COM  crystals  are  encapsulated 
within  early  endosomes  and  then  fused  with  lys-
osomes.  The  acidic  environment  of  the  lysosome 
may promote crystal dissolution, but excessive crys-
tal  accumulation  cannot  be  efficiently  digested  by 
the lysosome, thereby destabilizing the lysosome and 
inducing cellular stress and protease leakage into the 
cytoplasm [11, 60].

3)  COM  crystals  interact  differently  with  various  cell 

types.

  Different cell types also vary in their ability to inter-
act with COM crystals. Renal proximal tubular cells 
are highly sensitive to COM crystals [61]. Collecting 
duct  cells  exhibit  weak  binding  affinity  for  crystals 
[61].  Macrophages  remove  crystals  mainly  through 
phagocytosis [5].

COM crystal‑induced pyroptosis and polarization: size 
effect

1)  COM crystal-induced pyroptosis: the process.

  COM  crystals  rapidly  bind  to  the  cell  membrane, 
after  which  cells  internalize  the  crystals  through 
endocytosis or phagocytosis [11]. The cell membrane 
integrity  of  cells  adhered  by  crystals  is  destroyed, 
resulting  in  the  eversion  of  phosphatidylserine  and 
the  exposure  of  adhesion  molecules  (such  as  osteo-
pontin OPN and CD44), forming new crystal binding 
sites and forming a vicious cycle of adhesion–injury–
adhesion [59]. Crystals that are endocytosed by cells 
cause  organelle  damage,  such  as  lysosomal  damage, 
mitochondrial  damage,  and  endoplasmic  reticu-
lum  damage;  induce  ROS  overproduction;  activate 
NLRP3  inflammasome;  and  promote  the  release  of 
inflammatory factors [62]; all of these changes lead to 
pyroptosis.

  Adhesion  and  endocytosis  can  lead  to  cell  damage. 
The  damage  intensity  of  endocytic  crystals  is  gener-
ally  higher  than  that  of  crystal  adhesion  due  to  the

2)  COM crystal-induced pyroptosis: size effect.
  At  the  same  concentration  (0.5  mg/mL  COM  crys-
tals), COM-100 nm induced pyroptosis more signifi-
cantly than the other sizes (Fig. 4B). The reasons may 
be as follows. (1) The dispersed nanocrystals undergo 
extensive  endocytosis,  facilitating  their  transport  to 
the  lysosome,  where  they  are  degraded  into  oxalate 
ions  and  calcium  ions.  This  process  alters  the  ionic 
strength  of  the  lysosome,  disrupts  osmotic  pres-
sure  equilibrium,  and  destroys  lysosomal  integrity 
[64].  (2)  The  more  negative  zeta  potential  indicates 
(Fig.  7B,  compared  with  COM-500  nm)  that  COM-
100  nm  is  predisposed  to  aggregation,  so  the  actual 
particle  size  in  contact  with  the  cell  is  not  uniform. 
(3)  In  the  nanometer  range,  particles  behave  similar 
to chemicals, making surface chemistry very impor-
tant [10]. (4) In addition, we found that the propor-
tion  of  necrotic  cells  was  high  in  the  COM-100  nm 
group,  and  whether  necrosis  will  interfere  with  the 

expression  of  pyroptosis-related  indicators  remains 
unclear.  In  general,  there  is  some  signal  crosstalk 
between  pyroptosis  and  necrosis  [65],  as  well  as 
some  degree  of  crosstalk  between  multiple  modes 
of  cell  death  [66].  In  subsequent  studies,  the  cause 
of  pyroptosis  can  be  investigated  by  using  necrosis 
inhibitors  to  inhibit  cell  necrosis  [67].  However,  at 
the  same  concentration  (0.5  mg/mL  COM  crystals), 
large COM crystals induced a high cell survival rate 
(Fig. 4A), so we believe that comparing the pyroptosis 
rate of COM crystals of different sizes at this time is 
inappropriate.  Therefore,  pyroptosis  was  detected  at 
70% cell viability, and the results showed that COM-
10  μm  significantly  induced  pyroptosis  (Fig.  4C).  At 
the same cell viability (70% cell viability), the degree 
of  pyroptosis  induced  by  COM-500  nm,  COM-
2.5  μm,  and  COM-10  μm  showed  a  significant  size 
effect, that is, except for COM-100 nm, the larger the 
size,  the  more  severe  the  pyroptosis  and  the  higher 
the proportion of pyroptotic cells (Figs. 4, 5, 6). Fig-
ure  10  summarizes  the  damage  and  induced  polari-
zation  of  Mφs  by  small  (< 1  μm)  and  large  (> 1  μm) 
COM  crystals.  Moreover,  for  nanocrystals,  a  single 
cell is sufficient for phagocytosis; however, when the 
size of crystals is too large for a single cell to phago-
cytose them, multiple cells can act together [11, 68]. 
Thus,  in  Fig.  10,  multiple  nanocrystals  interact  with 
one cell, and one or more microcrystals interact with 
one or more cells.

kidney stones to reduce the degree of kidney damage 
and  prevent  the  deposition  of  calcium  oxalate  crys-
tals  in  the  kidneys  [69–72].  Hydroxymalonic  acid,  a 
small-molecule compound, can bind to the surface of 
COM crystals through specific intermolecular inter-
actions,  inhibit  the  growth  of  crystals,  impede  renal

3)  COM crystal-induced polarization: size effect.
  The  proportion  of  Mφs  polarized  into  M1/M2  cells 
induced by COM crystals of different sizes was com-
pared  by  detecting  cell  morphology  and  the  expres-
sion  levels  of  CD86,  iNOS,  CD163,  and  CD206.  At 
70% cell viability, COM crystal-induced polarization 
showed  a  significant  size  effect,  that  is,  a  larger  size 
resulted in a higher proportion of M1-type cells and 
a lower proportion of M2-type cells (Figs. 8, 9).
Inflammation  and  Mφs  infiltration  are  typical  pro-
cesses  associated  with  kidney  stone  formation  [74], 
and  renal  or  peripheral  Mφs  can  migrate  to  sites  of 
crystal deposition and phagocytose the crystals [75]. 
Crystals  interact  with  Mφs,  inducing  their  polariza-
tion and contributing to inflammatory responses. M1 
and  M2  Mφs  have  different  regulatory  roles  in  the 
formation  of  kidney  stones  [76].  M1  Mφs  can  pro-

mote  the  development  of  inflammation,  and  long-
term local inflammation can promote the formation 
of kidney stones [75]. By contrast, M2 Mφs has anti-
inflammatory and crystal phagocytic abilities, which 
can  reduce  renal  CaOx  crystal  sharpening  [77,  78], 
thereby lowering the risk of kidney stone formation.

Association of pyroptosis and polarization

At the same cell viability (70%), COM-10 μm induced the 
most severe pyroptosis, the highest proportion of pyrop-
tosis cells, and the highest proportion of polarization to 
M1  Mφs  compared  with  the  other  sizes.  There  may  be 
crosstalk  or  cross-regulation  between  pyroptosis  and 
polarization.

Macrophage  pyroptosis  and  polarization  often  occur 
simultaneously.  Macrophage  polarization  and  pyropto-
sis share common binding sites, signaling pathways, and 
outcomes  [79].  The  accumulation  of  ROS  is  an  impor-
tant  co-trigger  of  pyroptosis  and  polarization  [79–82]. 
NLRP3  inflammasome  activation  can  be  induced  by 
mitochondrial  ROS  generation,  mitochondrial  dysfunc-
tion,  and  oxidized  mitochondrial  DNA  [80],  followed 
by  pyroptosis.  Elevated  ROS  levels  mainly  facilitate  the 
phagocytic activity of M1 macrophages [81]. As a second 
messenger,  ROS  mediates  the  inflammatory  response  of 
M1 macrophages, which is primarily activated by MAPK, 
NF-κB, and inflammasomes [82]. The NLRP3 inflamma-
some is the core molecule linking pyroptosis and polari-
zation  [27,  83].  NLRP3  can  directly  activate  the  NLRP3 
inflammasome,  activate  GSDMD,  cleave  caspase-1,  and 
activate  and  release  IL-1β  and  IL-18,  leading  to  pyrop-
tosis  [33].  NLRP3  can  also  promote  the  polarization  of 
macrophages  to  M1  type  by  converting  danger  recogni-
tion into danger response by activating caspase 1, which 
cleaves  pro-IL-1β  into  its  bioactive  and  secreted  form 
and  promotes  macrophage  polarization  into  the  proin-
flammatory M1 phenotype [11].

Although the mechanism of the above process has not 
been fully explored, many studies corroborate it. Inhibi-
tion  of  NLRP3  and  ASC  in  mice  fed  a  high  oxalate  diet 
was found to reduce CaOx crystal deposition in the kid-
neys  and  alter  the  phenotype  of  renal  infiltrating  Mφs 
from  an  M1  pro-inflammatory  phenotype  to  an  M2 
anti-inflammatory  phenotype  compared  with  untreated 
controls  [84].  The  TLR/NF-κB  pathway  not  only  plays 
an  important  role  in  M1  polarization  but  also  induces 
pyroptosis  [85,  86].  Knockdown  of  CD38  promotes  the 
expression  of  molecules  related  to  M1  polarization  and 
triggers  severe  pyroptosis  [87].  In  mice  with  sepsis-
induced  acute  lung  injury,  alveolar  macrophages  are 
polarized  along  with  pyroptosis.  Alveolar  macrophage 
pyroptosis  is  related  to  the  polarization  of  alveolar  Mφ

Therapeutic strategies targeting pyroptosis or polarization

Despite the successful advancement of shock wave litho-
tripsy and endoscopic technology in the treatment of kid-
ney  stones,  the  incidence  and  recurrence  rate  of  kidney 
stones  remain  high. The  etiology  and  formation  mecha-
nisms  of  kidney  stones  have  not  been  fully  elucidated, 
and  effective  prevention  methods  are  lacking  in  clinical 
practice. At present, citrate, allopurinol, magnesium, and 
Chinese herbal medicine are often used as adjuvant treat-
ments  for  kidney  stones,  but  their  therapeutic  effect  is 
limited.

In  recent  years,  researchers  have  suppressed  the  per-
sistence  of  inflammation  in  various  disease  models  by 
decreasing pyroptosis and M1 polarization to inhibit dis-
eases [88–91]. However, this treatment strategy has rarely 
been mentioned in the prevention and treatment of kid-
ney stones and may guide our future research endeavors.
The  experimental  results  of  this  study  showed  that 
inhibiting  pyroptosis  and  regulating  the  polarization 
direction  are  viable  techniques  for  the  prevention  and 
treatment  of  kidney  stones.  Ba  et  al.  [92]  presented  a 
novel approach using engineered macrophage cell mem-
brane-coated  hollow  mesoporous  manganese  dioxide 
nanoparticles  (KM@M@M)  to  target  and  treat  COM-
induced  kidney  injury,  effectively  scavenge  ROS,  and 
inhibit  NLRP3  inflammasome  activation,  thereby  pre-
venting  pyroptosis  and  kidney  damage.  Ding  et  al.  [93] 
showed  that  vitexin  exerts  protective  effects  against 
nephrolithiasis by inhibiting pyroptosis activation, apop-
tosis,  EMT,  and  macrophage  infiltration.  This  work 
studied  the  mechanism  of  kidney  stone  formation  from 
the  perspective  of  calcium  oxalate  crystal-induced  mac-
rophage  pyroptosis  and  polarization,  offering  insights 
for the prevention  of calcium oxalate  formation and the 
design of targeted anti-stone drugs.

Conclusions
This  study  demonstrated  that  COM  crystals  induce 
pyroptosis  in  Mφs  by  activating  the  NLRP3/ASC/cas-
pase-1/GSDMD/IL-1β signaling pathway. The large size 
of  COM  crystals  is  correlated  with  an  elevated  rate  of 
pyroptosis  and  enhanced  M1  polarization,  indicat-
ing  that  large  COM  crystals  are  effective  in  inducing 
pyroptosis and M1 polarization and promoting inflam-
mation. This study elucidated the mechanism by which 
large-size  COM  crystals  induce  inflammation,  thereby 
enhancing  the  understanding  of  the  formation  of  kid-
ney  stones.  The  feasibility  of  reducing  the  dimensions 

of  COM  crystals  and  suppressing  M1  Mφs  to  prevent

design  of  Mφ-targeted  drugs  for  the  prevention  and 
treatment of stones. However, this study had some limi-
tations. Although we examined the effect of crystal size 
on  cytotoxicity,  we  must  acknowledge  that  the  poten-
tial influence of crystal morphology on Mφs response is 
unavoidable.
